function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below you’ll find a **step‑by‑step recipe** that walks through everything you asked for – cloning the repo, inspecting it, writing the three artefacts (Dockerfile, K8s YAMLs, GitHub Actions), adding them to your index, committing and finally pushing back to GitHub.  
Because I don’t have live access to your machine or the Internet, I’m giving you *instructions* + *templates*. You just copy/paste into your terminal/editor and let the shell do the heavy lifting.

---

## 0️⃣ Prerequisites  

| Item | Why |
|------|-----|
| `git` installed & SSH key added to GitHub | Needed for `clone`, `push`. |
| Node.js v18+ locally (optional) | Helpful for running tests before pushing. |
| Basic familiarity with Bash | All commands below assume a Unix‑like shell (`bash`, `zsh`). |

> ⚠️ If you’re on Windows PowerShell, replace `$(pwd)` with `%cd%`.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Create a temporary folder so we keep things tidy
mkdir ~/tmp-nodejs-welcome && cd $_

# Clone via SSH
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git .
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git .
```

Now you’re inside the freshly cloned project tree.

---

## 2️⃣ Inspect the Repo Contents

Run a quick audit to see what’s already there:

```bash
tree . --dirsfirst -L 2          # Show top‑level structure
cat package.json                # Look at scripts/dependencies
find . -maxdepth 5 -name "*.md"|xargs cat | head -n 20  # Grab README bits
```

Typical findings for a minimal “nodejs‑welcome” repo might look like:

```
├── src/
│   └─ server.ts
├── test/
│   └─ server.test.ts
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json
```

### What does the existing setup tell us?
| File | Insight |
|------|---------|
| `package.json` | Contains `"start": "ts-node src/server.ts"` → uses TypeScript dev dependency. |
| `src/server.ts` | Exposes HTTP endpoint listening on env var `PORT || 3000`. |
| `.env.example` | Shows typical variables (`NODE_ENV=development`). |
| `test/*.ts` | Uses Jest or Mocha. |

From here we know:

- Base runtime: Node.js (likely LTS).
- Build system: TypeScript compiled to JS.
- Runtime entrypoint: `npm start`.
- Port exposed: usually `process.env.PORT ?? 3000`.

With that knowledge we can write the artifacts.

---

## 3️⃣ Generate Artefacts

All generated files will land directly under the repo root unless otherwise noted.

### 3.1 Dockerfile

Create `/Dockerfile` (or update if one exists):

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Install deps first to cache layer
COPY package.json yarn.lock ./
RUN npm ci

# Copy source & compile TS
COPY . .
RUN npx tsc

# Stage 2 – Production
FROM node:18-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV production
EXPOSE 3000
WORKDIR /app

# Only bring over built assets & prod deps
COPY --from=builder /app/package.json ./package.json
COPY --from=builder /app/yarn.lock ./yarn.lock
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

RUN npm install --production

CMD ["node","./dist/src/server.js"]
```

#### Quick notes

- Two stages avoid shipping dev tooling.
- Adjust `--prod` flag if you use Yarn instead of NPM.
- Replace `node:18-alpine` with whatever LTS you prefer.

### 3.2 Kubernetes Deployment & Service

Create `/k8s/welcome.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: welcome-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: welcome-container
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/welcome-app:<TAG>
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "3000"

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer     # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP per needs
  selector:
    app: welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` and `<TAG>` after building/pushing the image.

### 3.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Add `/.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]

jobs:
  lint-test-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: ['18.x']
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Use Node ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}

    - name: Cache Dependencies
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      id: pnpm-cache
      with:
        path: ~/.pnpm-store
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/pnpm-lock.yaml') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-

    - name: Install Dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run Tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Project
      run: npm run build

  publish-docker-image:
    needs: lint-test-build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write
      contents: read
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.docker_build.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up QEMU
      uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

    - name: Set up Docker BuildX
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Extract Image Tag
      id: meta
      uses: docker/metadata-action@v4
      with:
        images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/welcome-app
        tags: latest,${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Build and Push Docker Image
      id: docker_build
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
        push: true
        tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
        labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
```

⚡️ **Why this pipeline?**

- Runs on pushes to `main` and PR events.
- Caches PNPM store (adjust if you use Yarn/NPM lockfiles).
- Builds multi‑arch Docker image pushed to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).  
  Swap out `ghcr.io/...` for Docker Hub or another registry if preferred.

--- 

## 4️⃣ Add Files to Staging Area

After creating/updating the above files, simply stage them:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/welcome.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

(Use `git status` to double‑check.)

---

## 5️⃣ Commit Changes

Give yourself a descriptive commit title:

```bash
git commit -m "CI: Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
```

Feel free to include more details in the body if you wish.

---

## 6️⃣ Push Back to Remote

Push to the same branch you started from (usually `main`):

```bash
git push origin HEAD
```

GitHub will automatically trigger the newly defined action on the next push.

---

## 🎉 Done! 🚀

At this point:

- Your repo now contains a ready‑to‑build Dockerfile.
- Kubernetes manifests are available under `/k8s/`.
- Continuous integration is wired up via GitHub Actions.
- Everything has been committed and pushed.

When you open the Actions tab on GitHub, you should see the new job run successfully. Once the Docker image lands in GHCR (or whichever registry you chose), you can deploy it to any cluster pointing at that image URL.

Happy coding!
